jehoshaphats-alliances.name: Jehoshaphat’s alliances
jehoshaphats-alliances.charge: Joining affinity with Ahab and going up with him to Ramoth-gilead against the word of the prophet; joining himself with Ahaziah to make ships
jehoshaphats-alliances.summary: Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord and taught the law through Judah, joined affinity with Ahab by marrying his son to Ahab’s daughter, and went up with him to Ramoth-gilead after the true prophet Micaiah had foretold defeat (2 Chronicles 18:1-16). Ahab disguised himself and sent Jehoshaphat into the battle in his royal robes, and only the Lord’s help saved him (2 Chronicles 18:29-31). Jehu the son of Hanani rebuked him for helping the ungodly, and when he later joined with Ahaziah to build ships, the Lord broke his works (2 Chronicles 19:1-3; 2 Chronicles 20:35-37).
offenseFull: Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1): he married his son Jehoram to Ahab’s daughter, and through that marriage the daughter of Jezebel brought Baal worship into the southern kingdom, where even righteous kings after that could never fully purge it out. After some years he went down to Samaria, and Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, good northern kingdom hospitality, and persuaded him to go up to Ramoth-gilead, a war Judah had nothing to do with. Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was and his people as Ahab’s people (2 Chronicles 18:2-3). You cannot join affinity with people just because they are your people; this was a war God had not sanctioned. Some men are friends for their own occasion and will not stay in the day of your trouble (Ecclesiasticus 6:7-8), and a friend cannot be known in prosperity (Ecclesiasticus 12:8).

He was making a bad decision in being with the wicked, yet the spirit was still on him: he asked to enquire of the Lord first, and when four hundred prophets said go up, he asked whether there was not a prophet of the Lord besides. Ahab said there was one, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him, which meant he told the truth (2 Chronicles 18:4-7). A rebellious people tell the seers to prophesy smooth things (Isaiah 30:9-11), and the time comes when men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3-4). Micaiah told them he saw all Israel scattered on the mountains as sheep with no shepherd (2 Chronicles 18:16), and Jehoshaphat went up anyway.

At the point of no return Ahab told him that he would disguise himself, but Jehoshaphat should wear his robes. The king of Syria had ordered his captains to fight no one but the king of Israel, and Ahab knew it; he was setting Jehoshaphat up for the kill. The captains saw the robes, took him for the king of Israel and surrounded him, and if it had not been for the Lord he would have died in Ahab’s place (2 Chronicles 18:28-31). Beware of a counsellor who counsels for himself, who tells you your way is good and then stands on the other side to see what will happen to you (Ecclesiasticus 37:8). After Ahab was dead he did it again, joining himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly, to make ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:35-36).
judgmentFull: The Lord helped him and moved the Syrians away from him (2 Chronicles 18:31), but his rescue was mercy, not approval. When he returned in peace, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and asked whether he should help the ungodly and love those who hate the Lord; therefore wrath was on him from before the Lord. Nevertheless good things were found in him, for he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God (2 Chronicles 19:1-3). We have to be careful not to bring wrath on ourselves or on the congregation; the Lord does not like that thing right there. Do not strive in a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10).

Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah prophesied that because he had joined himself with Ahaziah, the Lord had broken his works, and the ships were wrecked and never went to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:37). Good works are being done, and all praise for the leadership that labours before us; but the scripture says that if we join with those doing wickedness, the Lord will break our works. The marriage he made outlived him: Jehoram his son took the daughter of Ahab, walked in the way of the kings of Israel and killed all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4-6), and Athaliah later destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:10). The judgment on his alliances was written in his ships and in his grandchildren.

jehoshaphats-alliances.offense: Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1): he married his son Jehoram to Ahab’s daughter, and through that marriage the daughter of Jezebel brought Baal worship into the southern kingdom, where even righteous kings after that could never fully purge it out. After some years he went down to Samaria, and Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, good northern kingdom hospitality, and persuaded him to go up to Ramoth-gilead, a war Judah had nothing to do with. Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was and his people as Ahab’s people (2 Chronicles 18:2-3). You cannot join affinity with people just because they are your people; this was a war God had not sanctioned. Some men are friends for their own occasion and will not stay in the day of your trouble (Ecclesiasticus 6:7-8), and a friend cannot be known in prosperity (Ecclesiasticus 12:8).
jehoshaphats-alliances.judgment: The Lord helped him and moved the Syrians away from him (2 Chronicles 18:31), but his rescue was mercy, not approval. When he returned in peace, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and asked whether he should help the ungodly and love those who hate the Lord; therefore wrath was on him from before the Lord. Nevertheless good things were found in him, for he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God (2 Chronicles 19:1-3). We have to be careful not to bring wrath on ourselves or on the congregation; the Lord does not like that thing right there. Do not strive in a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10).

And after certain years he went down to Ahab to Samaria. And Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, and for the people that he had with him, and persuaded him to go up with him to Ramoth–gilead.

And Ahab king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Wilt thou go with me to Ramoth–gilead? And he answered him, I am as thou art, and my people as thy people; and we will be with thee in the war.
And Jehoshaphat said unto the king of Israel, Enquire, I pray thee, at the word of the Lord to day.

Therefore the king of Israel gathered together of prophets four hundred men, and said unto them, Shall we go to Ramoth–gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And they said, Go up; for God will deliver it into the king’s hand.
But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord besides, that we might enquire of him?

And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man, by whom we may enquire of the Lord: but I hate him; for he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil: the same is Micaiah the son of Imla. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so.
And the king of Israel called for one of his officers, and said, Fetch quickly Micaiah the son of Imla.

And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat either of them on his throne, clothed in their robes, and they sat in a void place at the entering in of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets prophesied before them.
And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah had made him horns of iron, and said, Thus saith the Lord, With these thou shalt push Syria until they be consumed.
And all the prophets prophesied so, saying, Go up to Ramoth–gilead, and prosper: for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king.

And the messenger that went to call Micaiah spake to him, saying, Behold, the words of the prophets declare good to the king with one assent; let thy word therefore, I pray thee, be like one of theirs, and speak thou good.
And Micaiah said, As the Lord liveth, even what my God saith, that will I speak.

And when he was come to the king, the king said unto him, Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth–gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And he said, Go ye up, and prosper, and they shall be delivered into your hand.
And the king said to him, How many times shall I adjure thee that thou say nothing but the truth to me in the name of the Lord?
Then he said, I did see all Israel scattered upon the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd: and the Lord said, These have no master; let them return therefore every man to his house in peace.
And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and will go to the battle; but put thou on thy robes. So the king of Israel disguised himself; and they went to the battle.
Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of the chariots that were with him, saying, Fight ye not with small or great, save only with the king of Israel.

And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, It is the king of Israel. Therefore they compassed about him to fight: but Jehoshaphat cried out, and the Lord helped him; and God moved them to depart from him.
And Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in peace to Jerusalem.

And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the Lord? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the Lord.
Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God.
And after this did Jehoshaphat king of Judah join himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly:
And he joined himself with him to make ships to go to Tarshish: and they made the ships in Ezion–geber.

For some man is a friend for his own occasion, and will not abide in the day of thy trouble.

jeremiah.name: Jeremiah
jeremiah.charge: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; be not afraid of their faces: speaking all that was commanded, though the word was a burning fire shut up in his bones and his own familiars watched for his halting
jeremiah.summary: Jeremiah, of the priests in Anathoth, was known and ordained a prophet to the nations before he was formed in the belly, and he prophesied from the days of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1:1-5). Told not to plead his youth or fear their faces, he spoke against kings, princes, priests and people through the stocks, the burned roll and the miry dungeon (Jeremiah 20:1-2; Jeremiah 36:23; Jeremiah 38:6). The Lord made him a fortified city against the whole land: they fought against him and did not prevail, and when the city fell the enemy set him free (Jeremiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 40:1-6).
offenseFull: Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, of the priests in Anathoth, a Levite city in Benjamin, and the word came to him from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem in the eleventh year of Zedekiah (Jeremiah 1:1-3; Joshua 21:17-18). The verse-by-verse teaching places his ministry at about 627 to 586 BC and calls him one of the mightiest prophets in the scriptures; he worked hand in hand with Josiah’s reform and lamented Josiah when he fell (2 Chronicles 35:25).

Before the Lord formed him in the belly He knew him, set him apart and ordained him a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:4-5). The teaching reads this with Paul, separated from his mother’s womb (Galatians 1:15), and the study note says the same thing is happening today: the brothers and sisters waking up were known from the beginning and are raised up to prophesy against the nations. Jeremiah answered that he could not speak, for he was a child, about eighteen by the teacher’s reckoning; the Lord told him not to say it, but to go where he was sent and speak what he was commanded, without fear of their faces (Jeremiah 1:6-8). The class puts it plainly: stop making excuses; he tried to run from it and the Lord did not let him. The Lord touched his mouth, put His words there, and set him over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant (Jeremiah 1:9-10). That is why we stay within these scriptures and never go wrong, the note says, and it is our job today, spiritual warfare. He was to gird himself and speak all he was commanded and not be dismayed, lest he be confounded before them; we cannot go out with a spirit of fear on us (Jeremiah 1:17; 2 Timothy 1:7).

The opposition came from his own. When he stood in the court of the Lord’s house and said the house would become like Shiloh, the priests, the prophets and the people seized him and said he must die; he answered that he was in their hand, but they would bring innocent blood on themselves (Jeremiah 26:8-16). Urijah, who prophesied the same words, was hunted down and slain by Jehoiakim, while the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:20-24). Pashur the priest struck him and put him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:1-2). Mocked daily, he resolved to speak no more in the Lord’s name, but the word burned inside him like fire trapped in his bones and he could not hold it in (Jeremiah 20:7-9).

One class reads those verses as his thoughts in the stocks, encouraging himself; the fire is inescapable, not surface level. His familiar friends watched for him to stumble (Jeremiah 20:10): the people who watched you grow up, waiting for you to revert so they can plaster it over social media. Jehoiakim cut the roll and burned it, and the words were written again with more besides (Jeremiah 36:23-32). The princes let him down into the dungeon of Malchiah and he sank in the mire (Jeremiah 38:6); the class says that mire is dung, and it is not far fetched.
judgmentFull: The promise of his ordination was kept: they fought against him and did not prevail (Jeremiah 1:19). He had the respect of a prophet and the contempt of a prophet, the teacher says; his own king, princes and priests gave him trouble for forty years and could not stop him, and he never lost his love for his people. Ebed-melech drew him out of the mire, and he stayed in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken (Jeremiah 38:7-13; Jeremiah 38:28). Nebuchadnezzar gave charge to look after him and do him no harm (Jeremiah 39:11-12); the teaching calls this the Lord’s mercy and grace, the enemies showing him favour, as the Lord had promised to make the enemy treat him well (Jeremiah 15:11; Proverbs 16:7).

Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told him the city fell because the people sinned and did not obey the voice of the Lord; the nations always knew why we went into captivity (Jeremiah 40:1-3; Judith 5:17-18). He had been bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, but he was loosed and given his choice, and he went to Gedaliah at Mizpah and dwelt among the people left in the land (Jeremiah 40:4-6). The verse-by-verse teaching stresses that Jeremiah was never a captive in Babylon. One class goes further, reading the word that he himself would lose his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he did not know as spoken to Jeremiah for the last days: that land, the class says, is called America today (Jeremiah 17:4).

text.text: The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin:
To whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.
Then the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things.
Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the Lord.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.

For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against the princes thereof, against the priests thereof, and against the people of the land.
And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the Lord, to deliver thee.

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, after that Nebuzar–adan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he had taken him being bound in chains among all that were carried away captive of Jerusalem and Judah, which were carried away captive unto Babylon.
And the captain of the guard took Jeremiah, and said unto him, The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place.
Now the Lord hath brought it, and done according as he hath said: because ye have sinned against the Lord, and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing is come upon you.

And now, behold, I loose thee this day from the chains which were upon thine hand. If it seem good unto thee to come with me into Babylon, come; and I will look well unto thee: but if it seem ill unto thee to come with me into Babylon, forbear: behold, all the land is before thee: whither it seemeth good and convenient for thee to go, thither go.

Now while he was not yet gone back, he said, Go back also to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon hath made governor over the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people: or go wheresoever it seemeth convenient unto thee to go. So the captain of the guard gave him victuals and a reward, and let him go.
Then went Jeremiah unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah; and dwelt with him among the people that were left in the land.
The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin:
To whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.
And out of the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon with her suburbs, Geba with her suburbs,
Anathoth with her suburbs, and Almon with her suburbs; four cities.

And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day, and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the lamentations.
Then the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace,
Then said I, Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the Lord.

Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them.

Now it came to pass, when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak unto all the people, that the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die.

Why hast thou prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying, This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord.
When the princes of Judah heard these things, then they came up from the king’s house unto the house of the Lord, and sat down in the entry of the new gate of the Lord’s house.
Then spake the priests and the prophets unto the princes and to all the people, saying, This man is worthy to die; for he hath prophesied against this city, as ye have heard with your ears.
Then spake Jeremiah unto all the princes and to all the people, saying, The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that ye have heard.
Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the Lord your God; and the Lord will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you.
As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you.

And they fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.
Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.
O Lord, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.
For since I spake, I cried out, I cried violence and spoil; because the word of the Lord was made a reproach unto me, and a derision, daily.

job.name: Job
job.charge: Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; and in all his loss he sinned not with his lips
job.summary: Job lived in the land of Uz but was not of that nation; he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam, as Israel lives among the nations today and is not of them. He sanctified his children after every one his day and offered for them in case they had sinned. Satan, who took his orders from the Lord and needed his permission, was given all that Job had and then his flesh, and Job blessed the name of the Lord and answered his wife that we receive both good and evil at the hand of God. When the Lord answered him he repented in dust and ashes and prayed for his friends, and the Lord turned his captivity.
offenseFull: Job was a man of the land of Uz, blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned from evil, the greatest of all the men of the east (Job 1:1-3). Living in the land of Uz did not make him of that nation, for he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam. Some say he was an Edomite on the strength of a paragraph the Greek copy adds at the end of the book out of a Syriac writing, making him Jobab of the kings of Edom; the Hebrew, the Latin and the English all end at the same place, and that addition is commentary, not scripture. Job settles it himself: his skin was black upon him (Job 30:30). The law of sacrifice was never given to Esau, yet the Lord sends three men at the end of the book to offer through Job (Numbers 28:1-2); Ezekiel ranks him with Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14, 20).

Job 29 shows who he was before the trial: he prepared his seat in the street as a judge, delivered the poor and the fatherless, and broke the jaws of the wicked (Job 29:4-17; Deuteronomy 16:18). His sons feasted in their houses, every one his day, which is their birthdays, the only birthdays the scriptures record being kept by the heathen; and Job offered burnt offerings for each of them, in case they had sinned in their hearts (Job 1:4-5; Job 8:4).

When the sons of God came before the Lord, Satan came among them (Job 1:6); the sons of God are the lineage of Adam, also called angels, for another word for angel is messenger. The Lord asked Satan whether he had considered his servant Job, since there was none like him. The more good works a man does, the harder Satan comes at him. Satan asked whether Job feared God for nothing, and whether a hedge had not been made about him; the hedge is the angel of the Lord that encamps round about them that fear him (Job 1:8-10; Psalms 34:7). He is subject to God and took his orders: all Job had was put in his power, but not Job himself (Job 1:12). Both good and evil come from the Lord, who makes peace and creates evil (Isaiah 45:7). In one day the Sabeans, fire from heaven, the Chaldeans and a great wind took his herds, his servants and all ten children (Job 1:13-19). Job tore his mantle, fell to the ground and worshipped: he had come naked and would return naked, the Lord had given and the Lord had taken away, and he blessed the name of the Lord; in all this he did not sin or charge God with wrong (Job 1:20-22). Then the Lord bragged on him, that he still held fast his integrity; Satan was given his flesh but not his life (Job 2:3-7). His wife told him to curse God and die: if Satan cannot get to a man he comes through his woman, as he went to Eve. Job answered that she spoke as one of the foolish women, and asked whether they should receive good at God’s hand and not evil (Job 2:9-10).
judgmentFull: When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind, Job laid his hand on his mouth; he had uttered what he did not understand, and having now seen with his eye what he had heard by the ear, he repented in dust and ashes (Job 40:4; Job 42:3-6). The Lord’s wrath was kindled against the three friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, and the sacrifice for their sin had to be carried to the righteous one in the matter (Job 42:7-9).

The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before, and seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, the fairest women in all the land, to whom he gave inheritance among their brothers. He lived a hundred and forty years and saw four generations (Job 42:10-16). James points to the patience of Job and the end the Lord gave, to show that the Lord is full of compassion and tender mercy (James 5:11). And Job looked past the restoration: he knew that his redeemer lived and would stand at the latter day upon the earth, and that though worms destroyed his body, in his flesh he would see God, with his own eyes (Job 19:25-27). His life is the pattern for every son of God: prepare the soul for temptation, for the trial comes by the Lord’s permission and inside his limits, and he will not suffer a man to be tempted above what he is able (Ecclesiasticus 2:1; 1 Corinthians 10:13).

text.text: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters.

His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east.
My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat.
And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying,
Command the children of Israel, and say unto them, My offering, and my bread for my sacrifices made by fire, for a sweet savour unto me, shall ye observe to offer unto me in their due season.
Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord God.
Though Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, as I live, saith the Lord God, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter; they shall but deliver their own souls by their righteousness.
As I was in the days of my youth, when the secret of God was upon my tabernacle;
When the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were about me;
When I washed my steps with butter, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil;
When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street!
The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up.
The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth.
The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth.
When the ear heard me, then it blessed me; and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me:
Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him.
The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow’s heart to sing for joy.
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem.
I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame.
I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out.
And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth.
Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.
And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.

And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.
If thy children have sinned against him, and he have cast them away for their transgression;
Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them.
And the Lord said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?
Then Satan answered the Lord, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?
Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
And the Lord said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord.
I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the Lord do all these things.
And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother’s house:
And there came a messenger unto Job, and said, The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them:
And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.

While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.

While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.
While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother’s house:
And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.
Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped,
And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.

And the Lord said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause.
And Satan answered the Lord, and said, Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life.
But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face.
And the Lord said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life.
So went Satan forth from the presence of the Lord, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown.
Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.
But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.
Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.
Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me.
I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.

And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.

Therefore take unto you now seven bullocks and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job.
So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job.
And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.

Then came there unto him all his brethren, and all his sisters, and all they that had been of his acquaintance before, and did eat bread with him in his house: and they bemoaned him, and comforted him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him: every man also gave him a piece of money, and every one an earring of gold.
So the Lord blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning: for he had fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.
He had also seven sons and three daughters.
And he called the name of the first, Jemima; and the name of the second, Kezia; and the name of the third, Keren–happuch.
And in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job: and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.
After this lived Job an hundred and forty years, and saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, even four generations.
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:
Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

jobs-friends.name: Job’s three friends
jobs-friends.charge: Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous, having found no answer
jobs-friends.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite came from their own places by appointment to mourn with Job and comfort him, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they reasoned from his suffering back to his guilt, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. The Lord answered them by name: they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had, and he sent them with sacrifice to the man they had condemned, that he might pray for them.
offenseFull: When Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had come on him, each came from his own place by appointment to mourn with him and to comfort him. They lifted up their voice and wept, rent every man his mantle, sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven, and sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word, for they saw that his grief was very great (Job 2:11-13). Friends who come to a man’s affliction with correction and hard truth are not the fault here. What is wanted is people who give straight facts and not people who butter a man up while he is in the wrong. The fault is the conclusion they reached and would not abandon.

Eliphaz began where it cuts deepest: Job had instructed many, strengthened the weak hands, upheld him that was falling and strengthened the feeble knees, and now that it had come on him, he fainted (Job 4:3-5). There is one that is wise and teaches many and yet is unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19): you were the man who comforted everybody, and now your own turn has come and you want to give up. That much was fair warning. Then he went further and asked who ever perished being innocent, or where the righteous were cut off (Job 4:7), which turns every affliction into proof of sin. Bildad asked whether God perverts judgment, pointed at Job’s dead children as cast away for their transgression, and promised a latter end that would greatly increase if Job were pure and upright, on the false premise that he was not already upright (Job 8:3-7; Job 1:1, 5). Zophar told him God exacted of him less than his iniquity deserved (Job 11:6). Then Eliphaz stopped inferring and began inventing: he said Job’s wickedness was great, that he had taken a pledge from his brother for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing and withheld bread from the hungry (Job 22:5-7), none of which the record supports. Job named it while it was being done: they were forgers of lies and physicians of no value and miserable comforters, and he asked whether they would speak wickedly for God and talk deceitfully for him (Job 13:4, 7; Job 16:2). Defending God with false accusations against his servant is the thing this case is entered for. Elihu’s wrath was kindled against the three because they had found no answer and yet had condemned Job (Job 32:3); and it was Elihu who spoke the word that reaches to our own day, that by reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry, and they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty (Job 35:9).
judgmentFull: The Lord told Eliphaz the Temanite that his wrath was kindled against him and against his two friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had (Job 42:7). The remedy was sacrifice and intercession, and it had to be carried to the man they had accused: seven bullocks and seven rams, brought to his servant Job, a burnt offering offered for themselves, and Job would pray for them, for the Lord would accept him, or else he would deal with them after their folly (Job 42:8). That is how the priesthood always worked in Israel: the sacrifice is brought to the righteous one and offered on the sinner’s behalf, and the man who does not bring it is not forgiven.

The three who had argued so long for Job’s guilt now depended on the prayer of the man they had condemned, and the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16). It was not the prayer by itself, but the prayer of a righteous man; the Most High deals with those who are dealing in righteousness. They did as the Lord commanded them, and the Lord also accepted Job; and it was in the praying for these friends that his own captivity was turned (Job 42:9-10). Afterward his brethren and sisters and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him and comforted him, every man bringing him a piece of money and an earring of gold (Job 42:11). The friends were restored along with everything else.

lawsResolved.text: Doing injustice by justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous is an abomination and condemned by God.
We should not speak evil of someone out of suspicions or assumptions.
You shall not lie to one another.
Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause.

text.text: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him.
And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven.
So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.

Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees.
But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled.

Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry.

jonah.name: Jonah
jonah.charge: Rising up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord instead of going to Nineveh to cry against it
jonah.summary: The word of the Lord sent Jonah the son of Amittai to cry against Nineveh, and he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord (Jonah 1:1-3). The storm found him asleep in the ship; he confessed he was the cause and was cast into the sea, and the Lord prepared a great fish in which he lay three days and three nights, praying, until he was put out on dry land (Jonah 1:4-17; Jonah 2:1-10). Sent the second time he went and cried against the city, and when the Lord spared it he was angry; the Lord reproved him with the gourd, and Christ made his three days the sign given to His generation (Jonah 3:1-4; Jonah 4:1-11; Matthew 12:39-40).
offenseFull: Jonah the son of Amittai prophesied in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, who restored Israel’s border by his word (2 Kings 14:25). The word came to him to go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for its wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Christians read Ninevites and think Assyrians, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were the captives of the ten tribes led into Nineveh, as Tobit of Naphtali shows, who was carried there and heard Jonah and took heed (Tobit 1:1-3; Tobit 14:8); the study note on Acts 1 likewise says Jonah preached to Nineveh, where the northern kingdom was exiled. Our people in Nineveh were observing lying vanities, one class says, as they keep Christmas and a white Jesus today (Jonah 2:8).

Jonah said no, as the teacher puts it: he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, went down to Joppa, found a ship, paid the fare and went aboard (Jonah 1:3). The study note on Genesis 10 places Tarshish in Spain, first among the merchants of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:12); one history teaching reads from a book that Jonah looked to it as a safe haven where Hebrew traders had been since Solomon’s time, and another says most place it at Sicily. Two classes say he fled because he was afraid of the people of Nineveh; he himself later says he fled because he knew the Lord was gracious and merciful and would relent (Jonah 4:2), and the teaching adds that he feared being taken for a false prophet. Both can stand; like Adam, one class says, he tried to hide.

The Lord sent a great wind and the ship was near breaking; the mariners cried each to his own god, and Jonah lay fast asleep in the sides of the ship (Jonah 1:4-5). The study note calls him the picture of the slack spirit, asleep while the ship breaks, and America the spiritual ship going down with our people asleep in it. The lot fell on Jonah, and he confessed he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord, the God of heaven who made the sea and the dry land (Jonah 1:7-10).
judgmentFull: He told them to throw him into the sea, for the storm was on his account (Jonah 1:11-12). That is accountability and integrity, the teaching says, owning that you are the cause, the opposite of Achan, whose hidden sin troubled the camp (Joshua 7:1). They rowed hard, prayed not to be charged with innocent blood, and cast him in, and the sea ceased her raging (Jonah 1:13-16). The Lord had prepared a great fish and Jonah was in its belly three days and three nights (Jonah 1:17). He cried to the Lord out of the belly of hell, which the teaching explains is the grave; cast out of His sight, he would look again toward the holy temple and pay what he had vowed (Jonah 2:1-9). The man who fled the Lord now sought Him, as in their affliction they will seek Him early (Hosea 5:15); in the fish, one class says, he repented of his fear and his doubt, and the teaching reads his rising from the pit as pointing to Christ, whose soul would not be left in the grave (Psalm 16:10).

The word came the second time, and he went and cried what he was given, that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 3:1-4). When the Lord spared the city he was very angry and asked to die (Jonah 4:1-3). Jonah had an attitude problem, one class says, self-willed, mad that God did not destroy the people, like James and John wanting fire from heaven (Luke 9:54-55). With the gourd, the worm and the east wind the Lord showed him that he pitied a plant he had not laboured for, and asked whether He should not spare Nineveh (Jonah 4:4-11). Your spirit is not right, the teacher says; we do not preach for our own glory, and His thoughts are not our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8). The Lord held off because His people were there, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the word still stood and the city was destroyed (Tobit 14:4).

Christ gave that generation no sign but the sign of Jonas: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, and one greater than Jonah was there (Matthew 12:39-41). Three days and three nights, the teaching says, rules out Good Friday to Sunday. Jonah is actually about us, one class says: the God who heard him in the fish does not change (Malachi 3:6), so pray.

text.text: Now the word of the Lord came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

But the Lord sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.

Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.
And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?
And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.
Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous.
And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.
Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them.

Wherefore they cried unto the Lord, and said, We beseech thee, O Lord, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man’s life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O Lord, hast done as it pleased thee.
So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging.
Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the Lord, and made vows.
Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
Then Jonah prayed unto the Lord his God out of the fish’s belly,
And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the Lord, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.

Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple.
The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head.
I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O Lord my God.

And Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.
But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry.

And he prayed unto the Lord, and said, I pray thee, O Lord, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.

jonathan.name: Jonathan
jonathan.charge: Stripping himself of his robe for the man whom the Lord would make king; standing between his father and David’s innocent blood; thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee
jonathan.summary: Jonathan’s soul was knit with David’s, and he loved him as his own soul; the same word describes the church, hearts knit together in love. The king’s son and heir stripped off his own robe and gave it to the shepherd, with his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle. He warned David of his father’s intent, spoke good of him to Saul and had a javelin cast at him for it, and went out to him in the wood at Ziph to strengthen his hand in God. His loyalty exceeded his own desires, and the kindness he asked for reached his lame son at the king’s table.
offenseFull: When David had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul; they made a covenant, and Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him and gave it to David, with his garments, even to his sword, his bow and his girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). Souls being knit is not speaking of anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church, whose hearts are comforted by being knit together in love (Colossians 2:2), and the body, knit together by joints and bands (Colossians 2:19). Note the estate of the two men: Jonathan was the prince and the heir, David was an armourbearer out of Bethlehem, and a true friend does not rejoice in standing higher. A faithful friend is a strong defence and the medicine of life, and he that has found such a one has found a treasure (Ecclesiasticus 6:14).

Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants that they should kill David; the Philistines could not get him, so now the king wanted Israelites to kill an Israelite. But Jonathan delighted much in David and told him plainly that his father sought to kill him, and told him to take heed until the morning, abide in a secret place and hide himself (1 Samuel 19:1-7). Jonathan would have been next in line for the throne, and you would think his loyalty lay with his father, but he saw that the spirit was not on his father, it was on his brother David. Do not be ashamed to defend a friend, nor hide from him in the time of his trouble (Ecclesiasticus 22:25). He spoke good of David to Saul: let not the king sin against his servant, who had not sinned against him and whose works toward him had been very good, for he put his life in his hand and slew the Philistine and the Lord wrought a great salvation for all Israel, which Saul saw and rejoiced at; so why sin against innocent blood and slay David without a cause? The innocent and righteous are not to be slain (Exodus 23:7), and hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17). Saul listened and swore that David would not be slain, and Jonathan brought him back. At the new moon, when David’s seat was empty and Jonathan covered for him, Saul’s anger was kindled against his own son, telling him that as long as the son of Jesse lived on the ground neither he nor his kingdom would be established, and he cast a javelin at him to smite him; by that Jonathan knew it was determined of his father to slay David (1 Samuel 20:30-33). He would not buy a throne with his friend’s blood. When David was hunted in the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan rose up and went to him into the wood and strengthened his hand in God, telling him not to fear, for the hand of Saul his father would not find him, and David would be king over Israel and Jonathan would be next to him, and Saul his father knew it too (1 Samuel 23:16-17).
judgmentFull: Jonathan had asked that the kindness of the Lord continue toward his house and never be cut off from it (1 Samuel 20:12-17). The covenant outlived him. The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua on mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). David lamented over them in the spirit, a eulogy and a prophecy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives and in their death they were not divided, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions; and

he was distressed for his brother Jonathan, whose love to him was wonderful, passing the love of women (2 Samuel 1:23-26). There is a friend that sticks closer than a brother (Proverbs 18:24); that is what Jonathan was. When David was king he asked whether any of the house of Saul was left, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, fetched Mephibosheth, lame on both his feet, out of Lo-debar, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:1-13). When seven of Saul’s house were delivered to the Gibeonites, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan because of the oath of the Lord that was between them (2 Samuel 21:7). Jonathan did not live to stand next to David, but his bones were gathered with his father’s into the sepulchre of Kish (2 Samuel 21:12-14), and the kindness he asked for was still being served at the king’s table years after he died.

text.text: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
And Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ;
And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.
A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found such an one hath found a treasure.
And Saul spake to Jonathan his son, and to all his servants, that they should kill David.

But Jonathan Saul’s son delighted much in David: and Jonathan told David, saying, Saul my father seeketh to kill thee: now therefore, I pray thee, take heed to thyself until the morning, and abide in a secret place, and hide thyself:
And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where thou art, and I will commune with my father of thee; and what I see, that I will tell thee.

And Jonathan spake good of David unto Saul his father, and said unto him, Let not the king sin against his servant, against David; because he hath not sinned against thee, and because his works have been to thee-ward very good:

For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the Lord wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?
And Saul hearkened unto the voice of Jonathan: and Saul sware, As the Lord liveth, he shall not be slain.
And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan shewed him all those things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence, as in times past.
I will not be ashamed to defend a friend; neither will I hide myself from him.
Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.
These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him:
A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood,

Then Saul’s anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said unto him, Thou son of the perverse rebellious woman, do not I know that thou hast chosen the son of Jesse to thine own confusion, and unto the confusion of thy mother’s nakedness?
For as long as the son of Jesse liveth upon the ground, thou shalt not be established, nor thy kingdom. Wherefore now send and fetch him unto me, for he shall surely die.
And Jonathan answered Saul his father, and said unto him, Wherefore shall he be slain? what hath he done?
And Saul cast a javelin at him to smite him: whereby Jonathan knew that it was determined of his father to slay David.
And Jonathan Saul’s son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.
And he said unto him, Fear not: for the hand of Saul my father shall not find thee; and thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth.

And Jonathan said unto David, O Lord God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about to morrow any time, or the third day, and, behold, if there be good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and shew it thee;

The Lord do so and much more to Jonathan: but if it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace: and the Lord be with thee, as he hath been with my father.
And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the Lord, that I die not:
But also thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the Lord hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth.
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, Let the Lord even require it at the hand of David’s enemies.
And Jonathan caused David to swear again, because he loved him: for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
And the Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchi–shua, Saul’s sons.
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.
Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet, with other delights, who put on ornaments of gold upon your apparel.
How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle! O Jonathan, thou wast slain in thine high places.
I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?
And there was of the house of Saul a servant whose name was Ziba. And when they had called him unto David, the king said unto him, Art thou Ziba? And he said, Thy servant is he.
And the king said, Is there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may shew the kindness of God unto him? And Ziba said unto the king, Jonathan hath yet a son, which is lame on his feet.
And the king said unto him, Where is he? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he is in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lo–debar.
Then king David sent, and fetched him out of the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, from Lo–debar.
Now when Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, was come unto David, he fell on his face, and did reverence. And David said, Mephibosheth. And he answered, Behold thy servant!

And David said unto him, Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father’s sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.
And he bowed himself, and said, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said unto him, I have given unto thy master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house.

Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him, and thou shalt bring in the fruits, that thy master’s son may have food to eat: but Mephibosheth thy master’s son shall eat bread alway at my table. Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

Then said Ziba unto the king, According to all that my lord the king hath commanded his servant, so shall thy servant do. As for Mephibosheth, said the king, he shall eat at my table, as one of the king’s sons.
And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Micha. And all that dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants unto Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king’s table; and was lame on both his feet.
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the Lord’s oath that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.

And David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh–gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth–shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, when the Philistines had slain Saul in Gilboa:
And he brought up from thence the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son; and they gathered the bones of them that were hanged.

And the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son buried they in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father: and they performed all that the king commanded. And after that God was intreated for the land.
The envious man hath a wicked eye; he turneth away his face, and despiseth men.

josiah.name: Josiah
josiah.charge: A tender heart at the reading of the book; rending his clothes; turning to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses
josiah.summary: Josiah began to reign at eight, sought the God of David while still young, and in his eighteenth year, while the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found (2 Chronicles 34:1-3; 2 Kings 22:8). When it was read to him he tore his clothes, and Huldah answered that the curses written in it would come, but because his heart was tender he would go to his grave in peace (2 Kings 22:11-20). He read the book to all the people, made a covenant, cleansed the land from the temple to Samaria, and kept a passover like none since the judges (2 Kings 23:1-25).
offenseFull: Manasseh began to reign at twelve, Amon at twenty-two and Josiah at eight, and the youngest was the wisest; better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13). He did what was right and turned neither to the right hand nor to the left, the charge given to Joshua (2 Kings 22:1-2; Joshua 1:7). In his eighth year he began to seek the God of David, and in his twelfth to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, groves and images (2 Chronicles 34:3-7). Jeremiah, a Levite and a priest’s son of Anathoth, was called in his thirteenth year, and Zephaniah prophesied in his days against the remnant of Baal (Jeremiah 1:1-2; Zephaniah 1:1-4).

In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan to have the silver given to the carpenters and masons repairing the house, and he made sure the workmen were paid, for the workman is worthy of his hire (2 Kings 22:3-7). Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law in the house of the Lord (2 Kings 22:8). Manasseh and Amon had been so wicked the very book was lost. When Shaphan read it, the king tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). The king was meant to read the law all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19), and the wicked kings had not. Josiah had been seeking the Lord for years and still had not heard the curses; what shook him was the wrath written for a people that will not listen (Deuteronomy 28:15). The same is true on the street today: people in Bible study their whole life know the Exodus, but never heard that the slave ships and the iron yoke are in the Bible.

He sent to enquire of the Lord, for great was the wrath kindled because the fathers had not kept the book (2 Kings 22:13). To enquire of the Lord you go to one who has the word. They went to Huldah the prophetess, who lived in Jerusalem in the college, the school where the sons of the prophets were trained in the scriptures, as the brothers go to the school on the Sabbath now. She answered that all the curses in the book would come on the place, as Micah had said Zion would be ploughed as a field for the sake of its heads, priests and prophets (2 Chronicles 34:22-25; Micah 3:9-12). But because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil (2 Kings 22:18-20).
judgmentFull: He gathered all the people, small and great, read in their ears the whole book of the covenant, stood by a pillar and made a covenant to keep the commandments with all their heart and soul, and all the people stood to it (2 Kings 23:1-3). Our forefathers had the Bible, and the king read it openly. Then he cleaned house: the vessels of Baal and the host of heaven burned at the Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the grove burned to powder, the houses of the sodomites by the temple broken down, Topheth defiled so no child could be passed through the fire to Molech, the horses given to the sun taken away, and Solomon’s high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom defiled (2 Kings 23:4-14). He burned bones on Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel as the man of God had foretold by name (2 Kings 23:15-16; 1 Kings 13:2). The priests of the high places in Samaria he killed on their own altars (2 Kings 23:19-20). It was a bloody path to redemption: the king who will set no wicked thing before his eyes destroys early all the wicked of the land (Psalm 101:3-8). This is repentance in action, cleaning house of every idol that brings a people under punishment.

He commanded the passover as written in the book, and none like it had been kept since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-22); reading the law brought the nation back to the appointed feasts in order, as the feast is kept in order today. No king before or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul and might (2 Kings 23:25). His memory is like perfume and like honey in every mouth; he behaved uprightly in the conversion of the people, and in a time of the ungodly he established the worship of God. All the kings except David, Hezekiah and Josiah were defective, for they forsook the law (Ecclesiasticus 49:1-4). Yet the Lord did not turn from His wrath over Manasseh’s provocations (2 Kings 23:26-27); the promise to Josiah was that the evil would not come in his days.

text.text: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem one and thirty years.
And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in the ways of David his father, and declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left.

For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father: and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images.
And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.
And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king’s, saying,

Go ye, enquire of the Lord for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.

So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
And she said unto them, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me,
Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read:

Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands; therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched.
But to the king of Judah which sent you to enquire of the Lord, thus shall ye say to him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, As touching the words which thou hast heard;

josiah-at-megiddo.name: Josiah at Megiddo
josiah-at-megiddo.charge: Going out against Necho king of Egypt who had no quarrel with him; hearkening not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God; disguising himself to fight
josiah-at-megiddo.summary: Some years after his great passover, Josiah went out against Necho king of Egypt, who was marching to Carchemish on the Euphrates to fight the Babylonians and told him plainly that his quarrel was not with Judah and that God was with him (2 Chronicles 35:20-21). Josiah would not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, disguised himself, and was shot by the archers in the valley of Megiddo; he died in Jerusalem and all Judah mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). He got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it.
offenseFull: Josiah’s passover was right on time, on the fourteenth day of the first month as Moses instituted it (2 Chronicles 35:1), and it was greater than any since the days of Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:18); his works were upright, with a heart full of godliness (1 Esdras 1:23). It shows what order and unity in righteousness can restore, even after all we had done and suffered. The same history shows the other lesson: you can know all the precepts and be righteous and still get high minded, and you have to mind your God-given business.

The power of Assyria was slipping, and Babylon and Egypt were contending for what it had held. Nineveh had fallen to the Babylonians and Medes, and Pharaoh Necho led his army north to help what was left of Assyria at Carchemish, passing through Josiah’s kingdom on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Josiah went out against him (2 Chronicles 35:20). Necho sent ambassadors asking what he had to do with the king of Judah: he had not come against him but against the house he was at war with, for God had commanded him to make haste, and Josiah should stop meddling with God, who was with him, lest God destroy him (2 Chronicles 35:21). The Lord is not restricted in whom He speaks through; He spoke through a donkey and through Balaam, and He had spoken to Pharaoh. That did not mean He wanted Egypt to stop Babylon, for He had already foretold in Hezekiah’s day that Babylon would take Judah (Isaiah 39:5-7). Pharaoh was telling his Israelite brother to fall back, because this had nothing to do with him.

In Josiah’s eyes he was standing up to possible Egyptian oppression. Nevertheless he would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself to fight, and did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God (2 Chronicles 35:22). Esdras says he did not regard the words of the prophet Jeremiah spoken by the mouth of the Lord (1 Esdras 1:28). Ben Sira warns not to strive in a matter that does not concern you, for if you meddle much you will not escape (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10), and the one who meddles with strife not belonging to him is like a man who takes a dog by the ears (Proverbs 26:17). Grab a pit bull by the ears and you are going to get torn up.
judgmentFull: He went into the battle in disguise, yet the archers shot at king Josiah himself. Pharaoh had warned that God would destroy him if he meddled, and among all the soldiers the Lord put it on the archers to find the king. He told his servants to take him away, for he was badly wounded; they moved him to his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in the sepulchres of his fathers (2 Chronicles 35:23-24). Megiddo is the place of troops, the place the Lord will gather all nations again in the last days. After Megiddo the Egyptians and Assyrians were destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, Assyria ceased to be, and Babylon rose to take Judah as the prophets had said; the Bible is real history.

All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah; Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in the same years as Josiah’s reform, lamented for him, and the singing men and women spoke of him in their lamentations and made it an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:24-25). The promise through Huldah that he would be gathered to his grave in peace concerned the evil coming on Jerusalem, which he did not live to see (2 Kings 22:20). He meddled in a matter that did not belong to him, but he never went after another god, and he left a very good example. Virtue leaves a memorial that is immortal: when it is present men take example from it, and when it is gone they desire it (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1-2). Like David, whose righteous legacy stands over his transgressions, Josiah’s is praised among the famous men whose bodies are buried in peace and whose name lives for evermore (Ecclesiasticus 44:1-15). His death opened Judah’s last years: the people made Jehoahaz king, and within three months Pharaoh had him in bands (2 Chronicles 36:1-4).

jotham.name: Jotham
jotham.charge: Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; doing according to all that his father Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord
jotham.summary: Jotham, son of Uzziah, reigned sixteen years and did right as his father had done, but he did not go into the temple as his father had; the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, cities, castles and towers, and put the Ammonites under tribute (2 Chronicles 27:3-5). He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6).
offenseFull: Jotham judged the people from the king’s house while his father lived as a leper in a separate house, so the last years counted to Uzziah were really his son’s (2 Chronicles 26:21). He was twenty-five when he began to reign in his own right and reigned sixteen years; he did right according to all his father Uzziah did, except that he did not enter the temple of the Lord (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He was like his father, industrious and a builder, but he did not make his father’s mistake of going in to burn incense as though he were a Levitical priest.

Yet the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:2). The high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there (2 Kings 15:35); since Solomon brought in the gods of his wives, the land was never the same. Micah began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, and this is the corruption he describes: they built up Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, the heads judged for reward, the priests taught for hire, the prophets divined for money, and still they leaned on the Lord and said no evil could come on them; therefore Zion would be ploughed as a field (Micah 1:1; Micah 3:10-12). A righteous king in Jerusalem did not mean the whole realm was clean, any more than the lower parts of the capital are clean today.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord and much on the wall of Ophel, and cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the forests (2 Chronicles 27:3-4). He cut down the forests and made towns; we always built castles, that is Judah. He fought the king of the Ammonites and prevailed, and they paid him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand measures each of wheat and barley that year and the next two, putting the heathen under tribute as his father had done (2 Chronicles 27:5).
judgmentFull: So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6). That is what Ezra did when he prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach it in Israel (Ezra 7:10), and it is the opposite of Rehoboam, who did evil because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14). That is why he had favour during his reign. The Most High was with our forefathers when they followed the commandments.

In those days the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah (2 Kings 15:37). Syria had been the northern kingdom’s oppressor, and now the two were joining against Judah; it began under Jotham and came to its height under his son. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, not in the field where his leper father lay, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 27:7-9). A good reign does not pass to the next by blood, and the son who followed him would burn his children in the fire.
