Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers.

He fought also with the king of the Ammonites, and prevailed against them. And the children of Ammon gave him the same year an hundred talents of silver, and ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley. So much did the children of Ammon pay unto him, both the second year, and the third.
So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God.
In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel began Jotham the son of Uzziah king of Judah to reign.
Five and twenty years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok.
And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord: he did according to all that his father Uzziah had done.
Howbeit the high places were not removed: the people sacrificed and burned incense still in the high places. He built the higher gate of the house of the Lord.
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the Lord his God, and went into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense.
And Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him fourscore priests of the Lord, that were valiant men:

And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the Lord God.

Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, from beside the incense altar.

And Azariah the chief priest, and all the priests, looked upon him, and, behold, he was leprous in his forehead, and they thrust him out from thence; yea, himself hasted also to go out, because the Lord had smitten him.

And Uzziah the king was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house, being a leper; for he was cut off from the house of the Lord: and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land.
Jotham was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name also was Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok.
And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord. And the people did yet corruptly.
He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, and on the wall of Ophel he built much.
Moreover he built cities in the mountains of Judah, and in the forests he built castles and towers.

He fought also with the king of the Ammonites, and prevailed against them. And the children of Ammon gave him the same year an hundred talents of silver, and ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley. So much did the children of Ammon pay unto him, both the second year, and the third.
So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God.
Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars, and his ways, lo, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
He was five and twenty years old when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.
And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David: and Ahaz his son reigned in his stead.
Howbeit the high places were not removed: the people sacrificed and burned incense still in the high places. He built the higher gate of the house of the Lord.
Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
In those days the Lord began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah.

laban.name: Laban and the changed wages
laban.charge: Changing his hired servant’s wages ten times, and giving the elder daughter in place of the younger
laban.summary: Laban of the house of Nahor, an idolater as his fathers were, received Jacob as his own bone and flesh, then took seven years of work for Rachel and delivered Leah, charged seven more, and changed the wages ten times over twenty years while the Lord blessed him for Jacob’s sake. When Jacob left, he pursued him seven days with the power in his hand to hurt him, and God came to him in a dream by night and told him to speak to Jacob neither good nor bad.
offenseFull: Jacob went up out of Canaan north and then east to Haran, back to the family Terah had left there when he brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldees, and Laban said he was surely his bone and his flesh, which in the scriptures means, we are family (Genesis 29:1-5, 14; Genesis 11:26-31). Jacob loved Rachel, beautiful and well favoured, and served seven years for her, and they seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her; men gather gold and silver and every goodly thing and then let it all go and fix their eyes fast on a comely woman, and many have run out of their wits for a woman and become servants for their sakes (Genesis 29:16-20; 1 Esdras 4:18-26). In the evening Laban brought him Leah, and in the morning it was Leah; his answer, that it must not be so done in their country to give the younger before the firstborn, was a rule he had known before he took the seven years (Genesis 29:23-26). He required seven other years (Genesis 29:27-30).

Laban had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob’s sake, and Jacob reminded him how little he had before he came, and that it was now increased to a multitude, and asked when he should provide for his own house also (Genesis 30:27-30). Jacob asked no gift. He set terms that could be checked in the open, the speckled and the spotted and the brown to be his hire, so that his righteousness would answer for him in time to come; and Laban agreed and that same day removed those very cattle into the hand of his own sons and set three days journey between them (Genesis 30:31-36). Then he changed the wages ten times. Jacob’s account, which Laban does not deny, is that but for the God of his father he would have been sent away empty: twenty years, the drought consuming him by day and the frost by night, and his sleep departing from his eyes (Genesis 31:7, 38-42). When Laban’s sons said Jacob had taken away all that was their father’s, Laban’s countenance was not toward him as before (Genesis 31:1-2). The Lord told Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and to his kindred, and he would be with him (Genesis 31:3). Laban pursued him seven days journey and asked why he had stolen his gods. That question tells what Laban was: an idolater of the house of Nahor, whose fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood and served other gods, the very kindred the Most High had separated Abram from (Genesis 31:23, 30; Joshua 24:2; Genesis 12:1).
judgmentFull: The pursuer was restrained before he could use the power he had. God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night and warned him to take heed that he speak not to Jacob either good or bad (Genesis 31:24). He admitted it to Jacob’s face: he had the power to do Jacob harm, but the God of Jacob’s father had spoken to him the night before (Genesis 31:29). He searched every tent and found nothing. Jacob answered that God had seen his affliction and the labour of his hands, and had rebuked him the night before (Genesis 31:42).

They made a covenant at the heap and the pillar, that neither would pass over it to the other for harm, and Laban rose up early, kissed his sons and his daughters, blessed them and returned to his place (Genesis 31:44-55). The record does not reduce him to poverty, and it does not need to. It shows a man with the power and the numbers to take everything, stopped in his sleep by one sentence, and Jacob walking away with the household and with the substance the Most High had preserved for him out of twenty years of changed wages.

text.text: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came into the land of the people of the east.
And he looked, and behold a well in the field, and, lo, there were three flocks of sheep lying by it; for out of that well they watered the flocks: and a great stone was upon the well’s mouth.
And thither were all the flocks gathered: and they rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again upon the well’s mouth in his place.
And Jacob said unto them, My brethren, whence be ye? And they said, Of Haran are we.
And he said unto them, Know ye Laban the son of Nahor? And they said, We know him.
And Laban said to him, Surely thou art my bone and my flesh. And he abode with him the space of a month.
And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
Now these are the generations of Terah: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran begat Lot.
And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees.
And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram’s wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor’s wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah.
But Sarai was barren; she had no child.

And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram’s wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.
And Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured.
And Jacob loved Rachel; and said, I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter.
And Laban said, It is better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man: abide with me.
And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
Yea, and if men have gathered together gold and silver, or any other goodly thing, do they not love a woman which is comely in favour and beauty?

And letting all those things go, do they not gape, and even with open mouth fix their eyes fast on her; and have not all men more desire unto her than unto silver or gold, or any goodly thing whatsoever?
A man leaveth his own father that brought him up, and his own country, and cleaveth unto his wife.
He sticketh not to spend his life with his wife, and remembereth neither father, nor mother, nor country.
By this also ye must know that women have dominion over you: do ye not labour and toil, and give and bring all to the woman?
Yea, a man taketh his sword, and goeth his way to rob and to steal, to sail upon the sea and upon rivers;
And looketh upon a lion, and goeth in the darkness; and when he hath stolen, spoiled, and robbed, he bringeth it to his love.
Wherefore a man loveth his wife better than father or mother.
Yea, many there be that have run out of their wits for women, and become servants for their sakes.
And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in unto her.
And Laban gave unto his daughter Leah Zilpah his maid for an handmaid.
And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?
And Laban said, It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn.
Fulfil her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years.
And Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week: and he gave him Rachel his daughter to wife also.
And Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah his handmaid to be her maid.
And he went in also unto Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him yet seven other years.
And Laban said unto him, I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry: for I have learned by experience that the Lord hath blessed me for thy sake.
And he said, Appoint me thy wages, and I will give it.
And he said unto him, Thou knowest how I have served thee, and how thy cattle was with me.
For it was little which thou hadst before I came, and it is now increased unto a multitude; and the Lord hath blessed thee since my coming: and now when shall I provide for mine own house also?
And he said, What shall I give thee? And Jacob said, Thou shalt not give me any thing: if thou wilt do this thing for me, I will again feed and keep thy flock:

I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.

So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come, when it shall come for my hire before thy face: every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and brown among the sheep, that shall be counted stolen with me.
And Laban said, Behold, I would it might be according to thy word.

And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.
And he set three days’ journey betwixt himself and Jacob: and Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks.
And ye know that with all my power I have served your father.
And your father hath deceived me, and changed my wages ten times; but God suffered him not to hurt me.
If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked.
Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.
This twenty years have I been with thee; thy ewes and thy she goats have not cast their young, and the rams of thy flock have I not eaten.
That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it; of my hand didst thou require it, whether stolen by day, or stolen by night.
Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.
Thus have I been twenty years in thy house; I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.

Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight.
And he heard the words of Laban’s sons, saying, Jacob hath taken away all that was our father’s; and of that which was our father’s hath he gotten all this glory.
And Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and, behold, it was not toward him as before.
And the Lord said unto Jacob, Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred; and I will be with thee.
And he took his brethren with him, and pursued after him seven days’ journey; and they overtook him in the mount Gilead.
It is in the power of my hand to do you hurt: but the God of your father spake unto me yesternight, saying, Take thou heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad.
And now, though thou wouldest needs be gone, because thou sore longedst after thy father’s house, yet wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?

And Joshua said unto all the people, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods.
Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
And God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night, and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad.
Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou; and let it be for a witness between me and thee.
And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar.
And Jacob said unto his brethren, Gather stones; and they took stones, and made an heap: and they did eat there upon the heap.
And Laban called it Jegar–sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed.
And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed;
And Mizpah; for he said, The Lord watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.
If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take other wives beside my daughters, no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee.
And Laban said to Jacob, Behold this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee;
This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness, that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap and this pillar unto me, for harm.
The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered sacrifice upon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread: and they did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.
And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place.
And Jacob loved Rachel; and said, I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter.
And Laban said, It is better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man: abide with me.
And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
And Jacob said unto Laban, Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in unto her.
And Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast.
And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in unto her.
And Laban gave unto his daughter Leah Zilpah his maid for an handmaid.
And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?
And Laban said, It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn.
Fulfil her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years.
This twenty years have I been with thee; thy ewes and thy she goats have not cast their young, and the rams of thy flock have I not eaten.
That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it; of my hand didst thou require it, whether stolen by day, or stolen by night.
Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.
Thus have I been twenty years in thy house; I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.

Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight.

And Laban answered and said unto Jacob, These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these cattle are my cattle, and all that thou seest is mine: and what can I do this day unto these my daughters, or unto their children which they have born?
Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou; and let it be for a witness between me and thee.
And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar.
And Jacob said unto his brethren, Gather stones; and they took stones, and made an heap: and they did eat there upon the heap.
And Laban called it Jegar–sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed.
And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed;
And Mizpah; for he said, The Lord watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.
If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take other wives beside my daughters, no man is with us; see, God is witness betwixt me and thee.
And Laban said to Jacob, Behold this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee;
This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness, that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap and this pillar unto me, for harm.
The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered sacrifice upon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread: and they did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.
And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place.

lamech.name: Lamech
lamech.charge: Taking two wives, the first in scripture; killing a man and boasting of it; claiming seventy-sevenfold vengeance
lamech.summary: Lamech of Cain’s line was the first man in scripture to take two wives. His house carried the trades of that line, the harp and the organ in one son and the working of brass and iron in another, which is the first making of weapons. He boasted to his wives that he had killed a man, with the weapon his own son had made, and claimed seventy and sevenfold against Cain’s sevenfold. He knew the commandment against killing and appealed past it. No sentence is recorded.
offenseFull: Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). This is the first time scripture records a man taking multiple wives, and it is the sons of the wicked who did it; in the beginning it was one wife, and the line of Seth in the next chapter is not read of doing so (Genesis 2:24; Genesis 5:3-5). His house carried the trades of Cain’s line. Jabal fathered such as dwell in tents and have cattle, Jubal fathered all such as handle the harp and the organ, and Zillah bare Tubalcain, an instructor of every craftsman in brass and iron, which is the first making of weapons (Genesis 4:20-22). Music and warfare both sat in that one household, and the Most High takes the credit for neither man but for the making: he says he created the smith that blows the coals and brings forth an instrument for his work, and created the waster to destroy (Isaiah 54:16).

Lamech told his wives that he had slain a man to his wounding and a young man to his hurt (Genesis 4:23). He did it with what was to hand, and what was to hand was what his own son had forged. He knew the commandment against killing was in force in his day; that is exactly why he appealed to Cain’s sevenfold and claimed seventy and sevenfold for himself (Genesis 4:24; Genesis 4:15). They knew the commandments in that time. The word the Most High had spoken to restrain bloodshed was turned into a man’s boast of his own vengeance, though vengeance belongs to the Lord (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19). What he was announcing is the rule his line has kept ever since: touch one of us and we answer seventy times over, a household or a whole city for one man, because we hold the weapons.
judgmentFull: Genesis records no sentence upon this Lamech. His speech stands as the testimony of Cain’s line, growing in violence and self-exaltation, before the account turns to Seth and to those who began to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:25-26). Two lines carry the same names and not the same spirit. Cain’s Lamech fathered a son of destruction; Seth’s Lamech fathered Noah, and named him for the comfort he would bring concerning their work and the toil of their hands, because of the ground the Lord had cursed (Genesis 5:28-29). Good is set against evil, and life against death, and all the works of the Most High are two and two, one against another (Ecclesiasticus 33:14-15). The line of Cain went on in wickedness until the sons of God mingled with it, the earth was filled with violence, and the flood came (Genesis 6:1-5; Wisdom of Solomon 10:3-4). The absence of a narrated punishment does not turn his claim into God’s promise; delay is not acquittal.

lamech.offense: Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). This is the first time scripture records a man taking multiple wives, and it is the sons of the wicked who did it; in the beginning it was one wife, and the line of Seth in the next chapter is not read of doing so (Genesis 2:24; Genesis 5:3-5). His house carried the trades of Cain’s line. Jabal fathered such as dwell in tents and have cattle, Jubal fathered all such as handle the harp and the organ, and Zillah bare Tubalcain, an instructor of every craftsman in brass and iron, which is the first making of weapons (Genesis 4:20-22). Music and warfare both sat in that one household, and the Most High takes the credit for neither man but for the making: he says he created the smith that blows the coals and brings forth an instrument for his work, and created the waster to destroy (Isaiah 54:16).
lamech.judgment: Genesis records no sentence upon this Lamech. His speech stands as the testimony of Cain’s line, growing in violence and self-exaltation, before the account turns to Seth and to those who began to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:25-26). Two lines carry the same names and not the same spirit. Cain’s Lamech fathered a son of destruction; Seth’s Lamech fathered Noah, and named him for the comfort he would bring concerning their work and the toil of their hands, because of the ground the Lord had cursed (Genesis 5:28-29). Good is set against evil, and life against death, and all the works of the Most High are two and two, one against another (Ecclesiasticus 33:14-15). The line of Cain went on in wickedness until the sons of God mingled with it, the earth was filled with violence, and the flood came (Genesis 6:1-5; Wisdom of Solomon 10:3-4). The absence of a narrated punishment does not turn his claim into God’s promise; delay is not acquittal.

text.text: And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:
And the days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years: and he begat sons and daughters:
And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.
And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.
And his brother’s name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
And Zillah, she also bare Tubal–cain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal–cain was Naamah.
Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy.
And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.
If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.
And the Lord said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.
And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the Lord.
And Lamech lived an hundred eighty and two years, and begat a son:
And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the Lord hath cursed.
Good is set against evil, and life against death: so is the godly against the sinner, and the sinner against the godly.
So look upon all the works of the most High; and there are two and two, one against another.
And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them,
That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.
And the Lord said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.
And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
But when the unrighteous went away from her in his anger, he perished also in the fury wherewith he murdered his brother.
For whose cause the earth being drowned with the flood, wisdom again preserved it, and directed the course of the righteous in a piece of wood of small value.
And Zillah, she also bare Tubal–cain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal–cain was Naamah.

lot.name: Lot
lot.charge: A just man, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked; pressing the strangers into his house and standing at the door
lot.summary: Lot was a just man, one that does what is lawful and right, and living in Sodom he vexed his righteous soul from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked. He sat in the gate, pressed the two angels into his house because he knew the men of the city, made them a feast, and went out to the door and shut it behind him to stand between the mob and his guests. When he lingered, the men took him by the hand, the Lord being merciful to him, and brought him out before the fire fell.
offenseFull: To be just is to do that which is lawful and right, which is a commandment keeper; and just Lot was a righteous man who, dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds (Ezekiel 18:5; 2 Peter 2:7-8). A righteous man cannot be at home in that conduct. He was Abram’s brother’s son, out of the same house that was called out of Ur of the Chaldees (Genesis 11:27, 31). Two angels came to Sodom at even while he sat in the gate; he rose up to meet them, bowed himself with his face toward the ground, and pressed upon them greatly to turn in to his house, because he knew the men of Sodom, and he made them a feast and they did eat. Angels have bodies and eat as men do; Abraham had fed three of them under the tree, and their appearance is likened to burning coals of fire (Genesis 19:1-3; Genesis 18:8; Ezekiel 1:13).

When the men of the city, old and young, compassed the house and demanded the men, Lot went out at the door, shut the door after him, and begged them as brethren not to do so wickedly (Genesis 19:4-7). He named the deed for what it was before the law was written at Sinai. They pressed sore upon him and came near to break the door, and the men put forth their hand, pulled him into the house and shut the door, and struck those at the door with blindness (Genesis 19:9-11). Then he went out and warned his sons in law to get up and get out of the place, and to them he seemed as one that mocked (Genesis 19:12-14).
judgmentFull: While he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand and upon the hand of his wife and of his two daughters, the Lord being merciful to him, and brought him out and set him outside the city, and told him to escape for his life, not to look behind him, not to stay in all the plain, and to escape to the mountain (Genesis 19:15-17). The angel could do nothing until he had come to Zoar; the judgment of a whole plain waited on one righteous man being brought out (Genesis 19:22). The Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptations and to reserve the unjust to the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9). God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow (Genesis 19:29). Noah, Daniel and Job are named as men who deliver their own souls by their righteousness, and that is what Lot did; the sons in law who laughed did not, and no man’s righteousness covered them (Ezekiel 14:14).

Afterward he feared to dwell in Zoar and went up into the mountain with his two daughters, and dwelt in a cave. They thought Sodom had been the whole world and that there was not a man left in the earth to come in to them, so they made their father drink wine and lay with him, the firstborn one night and the younger the next, and he perceived it not when they lay down nor when they arose (Genesis 19:30-36). Take no wayward idea from it: uncovering the nakedness of a father was unlawful then and is unlawful now (Leviticus 18:7). The firstborn bare Moab, the father of the Moabites, and the younger bare Benammi, the father of the children of Ammon, to this day; in this teaching those nations are identified with the peoples known today as the Chinese and the Japanese (Genesis 19:37-38).

text.text: But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right,
And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:
(For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)
The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:
Now these are the generations of Terah: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran begat Lot.

And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram’s wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.
And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom: and Lot seeing them rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground;

And he said, Behold now, my lords, turn in, I pray you, into your servant’s house, and tarry all night, and wash your feet, and ye shall rise up early, and go on your ways. And they said, Nay; but we will abide in the street all night.
And he pressed upon them greatly; and they turned in unto him, and entered into his house; and he made them a feast, and did bake unleavened bread, and they did eat.
And he took butter, and milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them; and he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat.

As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps: it went up and down among the living creatures; and the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning.
But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:
And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.
And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,
And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.

And they said, Stand back. And they said again, This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge: now will we deal worse with thee, than with them. And they pressed sore upon the man, even Lot, and came near to break the door.
But the men put forth their hand, and pulled Lot into the house to them, and shut to the door.
And they smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great: so that they wearied themselves to find the door.
And the men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any besides? son in law, and thy sons, and thy daughters, and whatsoever thou hast in the city, bring them out of this place:
For we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the Lord; and the Lord hath sent us to destroy it.

And Lot went out, and spake unto his sons in law, which married his daughters, and said, Up, get you out of this place; for the Lord will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.
And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot, saying, Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters, which are here; lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city.

And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the Lord being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.

And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.
Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither. Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.
Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord God.
And Lot went up out of Zoar, and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he feared to dwell in Zoar: and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters.
And the firstborn said unto the younger, Our father is old, and there is not a man in the earth to come in unto us after the manner of all the earth:
Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.
And they made their father drink wine that night: and the firstborn went in, and lay with her father; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.

And it came to pass on the morrow, that the firstborn said unto the younger, Behold, I lay yesternight with my father: let us make him drink wine this night also; and go thou in, and lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.
And they made their father drink wine that night also: and the younger arose, and lay with him; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.
Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father.
And the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Moab: the same is the father of the Moabites unto this day.
And the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Ben–ammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day.
The nakedness of thy father, or the nakedness of thy mother, shalt thou not uncover: she is thy mother; thou shalt not uncover her nakedness.
And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,
And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.

Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do ye to them as is good in your eyes: only unto these men do nothing; for therefore came they under the shadow of my roof.
But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:
And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.

lots-wife.name: Lot’s wife
lots-wife.charge: Looking back toward Sodom against the angel’s command
lots-wife.summary: The angels told them to escape for their lives and not look behind them. Brought out of the city by the hand, his wife looked back from behind him and became a pillar of salt, a standing monument of an unbelieving soul. She looked back because she loved what was burning; for her to look back at all says she had never agreed to leave. Christ made her a proverb in three words: Remember Lot’s wife.
offenseFull: The instruction came with the rescue and it was specific: escape for your life, look not behind you, stay not in all the plain, escape to the mountain, or be consumed (Genesis 19:17). She had already been taken out by the hand together with her husband and her two daughters, the Lord being merciful to them (Genesis 19:16). The city she was leaving was the city whose men, old and young, from every quarter, had compassed her own house to know the two strangers, and had pressed against her own door (Genesis 19:4-7). Yet she looked back from behind him, against the word given to her (Genesis 19:26).

Ask why any woman would look back at that. The place was not a ruin: it was rich, glorious, full of the things the eyes want, and she loved that life. Somebody in that house was not vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked (2 Peter 2:7-8). For her to turn at all says she had never agreed to leave in the first place; she was grieving what was burning. Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world, for all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not of the Father but is of the world, and the world passes away (1 John 2:15-17). The psalm asks who will rise up for the Lord against the evildoers and who will stand up against the workers of iniquity, and she had not (Psalms 94:16).
judgmentFull: She became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). Wisdom keeps that standing pillar as a monument of an unbelieving soul, and the waste land that smokes as a testimony of the wickedness to this day (Wisdom of Solomon 10:6-7). Christ set her among the weightiest words in the scriptures. He said it would be as in the days of Lot, when they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and builded, until the same day that Lot went out of Sodom and it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all; and so shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed, and in that day the man upon the housetop is not to come down for his goods, nor the man in the field to turn back. Remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:28-32).

Babylon has an end, and whoever wants to carry Babylon into the kingdom is looking back the way she looked back; a man that puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). She was not left behind. She was led out by the hand, by angels, ahead of the fire, with the mercy of the Lord upon her, and still she did not make it, because being led out is not the end of obedience.

Remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:28-32).

No man, having put his hand to the plow (to follow and serve God), and then looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.

text.text: And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.

And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the Lord being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.
But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:
And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.
And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,
And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.
But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked:
(For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?
When the ungodly perished, she delivered the righteous man, who fled from the fire which fell down upon the five cities.

Of whose wickedness even to this day the waste land that smoketh is a testimony, and plants bearing fruit that never come to ripeness: and a standing pillar of salt is a monument of an unbelieving soul.
Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded;
But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all.
Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed.
In that day, he which shall be upon the housetop, and his stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back.
Remember Lot’s wife.
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
In that day, he which shall be upon the housetop, and his stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back.
Remember Lot’s wife.
Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it; and whosoever shall lose his life shall preserve it.
Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded;
But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all.
Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed.

mary-the-mother-of-jesus.name: Mary, the mother of Jesus
mary-the-mother-of-jesus.charge: Be it unto me according to thy word; blessed is she that believed
mary-the-mother-of-jesus.summary: The angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. She was told she would bring forth a son and call his name Jesus, that he would be great and be called the Son of the Highest, and that with God nothing shall be impossible; she asked how it should be, and then answered as the handmaid of the Lord, that it be to her according to his word (Luke 1:26-38). Elisabeth gave the verdict on that answer: blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:39-45).
offenseFull: Her answer was the answer of a servant. She called herself the handmaid of the Lord and said, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). The same messenger had stood in the temple six months earlier and told Zacharias that his wife would bear a son, and the promise was performed in its season, in the order the Most High set, and the same order holds here (Luke 1:13; Luke 1:23-24). Mary went from there into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah, and saluted Elisabeth, who was then six months with child (Luke 1:39-40).

Everything done for the child was done after the law. He was circumcised when eight days were accomplished and his name was called Jesus, as the law of circumcision requires on the eighth day, a covenant older than the Levitical priesthood and given to Abraham (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:3; Genesis 17:9-12; John 7:22). When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which is the offering the law appoints for a woman who cannot bring a lamb (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). He was made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those that were under the law (Galatians 4:4-5), and his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover (Luke 2:41). She kept the sayings spoken of him and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2:19). At the marriage in Cana she told him they had no wine, and when he answered that his hour was not yet come she turned to the servants and told them to do whatever he said (John 2:1-5). After the ascension she is named in the upper room with the eleven and the women and his brethren, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication (Acts 1:14).
judgmentFull: Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, called her blessed among women and blessed for believing, because there should be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:41-45). Mary answered with the song that magnifies the Lord for regarding the low estate of his handmaiden, and said that from that time all generations would call her blessed (Luke 1:46-48). The song does not stop with her. Her song says that God had shown the strength of his arm against the proud, brought the mighty down from their thrones and lifted the lowly, fed the hungry and sent the rich away empty, and helped Israel his servant in remembrance of his mercy, as he had promised the fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever (Luke 1:51-55). The mercy she was given is the mercy promised to the nation she belonged to.

Christ himself fixed where the honour goes. When a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bare him, he answered that rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27-28), and when he was told his mother and his brethren stood outside, he said that his mother and his brethren are those who hear the word of God and do it (Luke 8:21). He turned the honour off the mother and onto the keeping of the word, which is the same thing his mother had done at Cana when she pointed the servants at him. And the blessing came with a sword in it. Simeon told her that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul also (Luke 2:34-35). John places her standing by the cross, and records the care of her committed to the disciple whom he loved (John 19:25-27). She was called blessed, and she was not spared the grief that came with it.

text.text: And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth,
To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.
And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.
And when she saw him, she was troubled at his saying, and cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be.
And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God.
And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS.
He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David:
And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.
Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?

And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren.
For with God nothing shall be impossible.
And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.
And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Juda;
And entered into the house of Zacharias, and saluted Elisabeth.
And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:
And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.
And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy.
And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.
And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.
But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.
And it came to pass, that, as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished, he departed to his own house.
And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived, and hid herself five months, saying,
And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Juda;
And entered into the house of Zacharias, and saluted Elisabeth.
And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
And in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
And God said unto Abraham, Thou shalt keep my covenant therefore, thou, and thy seed after thee in their generations.
This is my covenant, which ye shall keep, between me and you and thy seed after thee; Every man child among you shall be circumcised.
And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every man child in your generations, he that is born in the house, or bought with money of any stranger, which is not of thy seed.
Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; (not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man.
And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord;
(As it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;)
And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

And when the days of her purifying are fulfilled, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, unto the priest:
Who shall offer it before the Lord, and make an atonement for her; and she shall be cleansed from the issue of her blood. This is the law for her that hath born a male or a female.

And if she be not able to bring a lamb, then she shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons; the one for the burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make an atonement for her, and she shall be clean.
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.
But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.
And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there:
And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.
And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine.
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.
These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.
And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:
And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.
And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy.
And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.
And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord,
And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.
He hath shewed strength with his arm; he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.
He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy;
As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.
And it came to pass, as he spake these things, a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked.
But he said, Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.
And he answered and said unto them, My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it.
And Simeon blessed them, and said unto Mary his mother, Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against;
(Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.
Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.
When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son!
Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

mephibosheth.name: Mephibosheth
mephibosheth.charge: What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am? and, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace
mephibosheth.summary: He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, because a new king customarily killed the descendants of the old one, and in her haste he fell and became lame. David fetched him out of Lo-debar for Jonathan’s sake, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually. When David fled from Absalom, his servant Ziba slandered him and took the estate; when the king came again in peace, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven and said, let him take all.
offenseFull: Jonathan the son of Saul had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she made haste to flee he fell and became lame; his name was Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4). She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill the descendants of the former king, so that none could overthrow him. But David asked whether there was yet any left of the house of Saul, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, because they had made a covenant, loving each other as their own souls (1 Samuel 18:3). Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, told him that Jonathan had yet a son, lame on his feet, in Lo-debar, and the king sent and fetched him. When Mephibosheth came he fell on his face and did reverence, and David told him to fear not, for he would surely show him kindness for Jonathan his father’s sake, restore him all the land of Saul, and have him eat bread at the king’s table continually; and he bowed and asked what his servant was, that the king should look upon such a dead dog as he (2 Samuel 9:1-8). His standing rested on a covenant between his father and the king, not on anything he could do.

During Absalom’s rebellion Ziba met David past the top of the hill with asses saddled and bread and raisins and summer fruits and wine; when the king asked where his master’s son was, Ziba said he abode in Jerusalem, saying that the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father that day. It was not true, and on that word David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:1-4). When the king came again, Mephibosheth came down to meet him, having neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace: he had mourned the whole time. He told the king that his servant had deceived him, for he was lame and had asked for an ass to be saddled that he might ride to the king, and Ziba had slandered him; but the king was as an angel of God, and all his father’s house were but dead men before the king, yet he had set his servant among them that ate at his own table, so he had no right to cry any more to the king. When David said that he and Ziba should divide the land, Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take all, forasmuch as his lord the king was come again in peace to his own house (2 Samuel 19:24-30).
judgmentFull: The king called Ziba and told him he had given his master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house; Ziba, his sons and his servants were to till the land and bring in the fruits, that his master’s son might have food, but Mephibosheth would eat bread always at the king’s table. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Samuel 9:9-13). That shows the riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, all set to work the land for a lame man out of the respect David had for Jonathan. So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet. This is what we need to bring back into Israel, that same love and care for the people we lose: we take care of their family as if they were there themselves. That is a large part of why the Most High called David a man after His own heart.

When the famine came for Saul’s bloody house and the Gibeonites required seven of his sons, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, because of the oath of the Lord between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). Set the two houses side by side. Saul had given his word to the Gibeonites and gone back on it, and the whole house paid for it, because when a man vows a vow to God he must not defer to pay it, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). David had given his word to Jonathan and kept it, and Jonathan’s crippled son was pulled out of that judgment by the promise. Jonathan was gone, Saul’s rule was gone, the kingdom had passed; the word of kindness had not passed, and a lame man at the king’s table made a kept promise visible every day.

But David asked whether there was yet any left of the house of Saul, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, because they had made a covenant, loving each other as their own souls (1 Samuel 18:3). Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, told him that Jonathan had yet a son, lame on his feet, in Lo-debar, and the king sent and fetched him. When Mephibosheth came he fell on his face and did reverence, and David told him to fear not, for he would surely show him kindness for Jonathan his father’s sake, restore him all the land of Saul, and have him eat bread at the king’s table continually; and he bowed and asked what his servant was, that the king should look upon such a dead dog as he (2 Samuel 9:1-8). His standing rested on a covenant between his father and the king, not on anything he could do.
mephibosheth.judgment: The king called Ziba and told him he had given his master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house; Ziba, his sons and his servants were to till the land and bring in the fruits, that his master’s son might have food, but Mephibosheth would eat bread always at the king’s table. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Samuel 9:9-13). That shows the riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, all set to work the land for a lame man out of the respect David had for Jonathan. So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet. This is what we need to bring back into Israel, that same love and care for the people we lose: we take care of their family as if they were there themselves. That is a large part of why the Most High called David a man after His own heart.

text.text: And Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
And David said, Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?
And there was of the house of Saul a servant whose name was Ziba. And when they had called him unto David, the king said unto him, Art thou Ziba? And he said, Thy servant is he.
And the king said, Is there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may shew the kindness of God unto him? And Ziba said unto the king, Jonathan hath yet a son, which is lame on his feet.
And the king said unto him, Where is he? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he is in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lo–debar.
Then king David sent, and fetched him out of the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, from Lo–debar.
Now when Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, was come unto David, he fell on his face, and did reverence. And David said, Mephibosheth. And he answered, Behold thy servant!

And David said unto him, Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father’s sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.
And he bowed himself, and said, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?

And when David was a little past the top of the hill, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of asses saddled, and upon them two hundred loaves of bread, and an hundred bunches of raisins, and an hundred of summer fruits, and a bottle of wine.

And the king said unto Ziba, What meanest thou by these? And Ziba said, The asses be for the king’s household to ride on; and the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat; and the wine, that such as be faint in the wilderness may drink.
And the king said, And where is thy master’s son? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father.
Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee that I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king.

And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.
And it came to pass, when he was come to Jerusalem to meet the king, that the king said unto him, Wherefore wentest not thou with me, Mephibosheth?
And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant is lame.
And he hath slandered thy servant unto my lord the king; but my lord the king is as an angel of God: do therefore what is good in thine eyes.

For all of my father’s house were but dead men before my lord the king: yet didst thou set thy servant among them that did eat at thine own table. What right therefore have I yet to cry any more unto the king?
And the king said unto him, Why speakest thou any more of thy matters? I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land.
And Mephibosheth said unto the king, Yea, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace unto his own house.
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said unto him, I have given unto thy master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house.

Thou therefore, and thy sons, and thy servants, shall till the land for him, and thou shalt bring in the fruits, that thy master’s son may have food to eat: but Mephibosheth thy master’s son shall eat bread alway at my table. Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

Then said Ziba unto the king, According to all that my lord the king hath commanded his servant, so shall thy servant do. As for Mephibosheth, said the king, he shall eat at my table, as one of the king’s sons.
And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Micha. And all that dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants unto Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king’s table; and was lame on both his feet.
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the Lord’s oath that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

mordecai-and-esther.name: Mordecai and Esther
mordecai-and-esther.charge: Mordecai: bowing not to Haman, nor doing him reverence. Esther: gathering the Jews to fast three days, and going in to the king not according to the law: if I perish, I perish
mordecai-and-esther.summary: Mordecai would not bow to Haman, and when Haman’s wrath became a decree against all the Jews he mourned in sackcloth, prayed, and charged Esther to go in to the king for her people (Esther 3:2; Esther 4:1-8; Rest of Esther 13:8-18). Esther feared the law against coming to the king uncalled, but at Mordecai’s word she had the Jews of Shushan fast three days with her, prayed, and went in against the law, ready to perish (Esther 4:10-16; Rest of Esther 14:1-19). God turned the king’s heart, Haman fell, the Jews were delivered, Purim was ordained, and Mordecai was made next to the king (Esther 7:10; Esther 9:1-32; Esther 10:3).
offenseFull: All the king’s servants bowed to Haman, but Mordecai would not bow, for he had told them he was a Jew (Esther 3:2-4). The class teaches that it is not our custom to bow to any man, the same as the three Hebrew children would not bow to the image. Mordecai’s own prayer gives the reason: not contempt, pride, or a desire for glory; he could have kissed the soles of Haman’s feet for the salvation of Israel, but he would not set the glory of man above the glory of God (Rest of Esther 13:12-14). The teaching sets it beside our people at work today, where the co-worker asks in front of everyone why you dress as you do and keep the Sabbath, and then goes to the supervisor.

When Mordecai learned of the decree he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried out through the city, and in every province there was mourning, fasting, and weeping (Esther 4:1-3). This was a law passed to kill every Israelite, and the teaching warns that such laws will be passed again. He prayed that the whole world is in God’s power and that if He has appointed to save Israel no man can stand against it, and all Israel cried out with him (Rest of Esther 13:8-18). He refused the clothes Esther sent and gave her messenger a copy of the decree, charging her to go to the king for her people (Esther 4:4-8).
Esther answered that whoever came to the king uncalled died unless he held out the golden sceptre, and she had not been called in thirty

days (Esther 4:10-11); the study note says she made an excuse. Mordecai would not take a weak answer: she would not escape in the king’s house more than the other Jews; if she kept silent, deliverance would come from another place and she and her father’s house would perish; and who could say she had not come to the kingdom for such a time as this (Esther 4:13-14). The deliverance of Israel cannot be held back, and the teaching applies it to anyone slothful in the work: the Lord will raise up somebody else. Esther had all the Jews in Shushan fast three days, she and her maidens with them, and resolved to go in against the law, and if she perished, she perished (Esther 4:15-17). She put off her royal apparel for mourning, covered her head with ashes, confessed that Israel was given to its enemies for worshipping their gods, asked for boldness and eloquent speech, and told God she abhorred the sign of her high estate (Rest of Esther 14:1-19). The teaching notes she was raised right, taught from her youth how the Lord took Israel from among all people.
judgmentFull: On the third day she put on her royal apparel and stood in the inner court; the king looked on her fiercely and she fainted, and God changed his spirit into mildness, so that he held out the golden sceptre and comforted her (Esther 5:1-2; Rest of Esther 15:1-16). At her second banquet she named Haman, and he was hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai (Esther 7:3-10). The king gave Esther the house of Haman and Mordecai his ring, and a second decree let the Jews in every city stand for their lives (Esther 8:1-11). Mordecai went out in royal blue and white with a great crown of gold, and many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell on them (Esther 8:15-17): a picture, the study note says, of the time when the fear of Israel will be on all nations.

The day their enemies hoped to rule them was turned the other way, and no man could stand before them (Esther 9:1-2). Mordecai and Esther wrote to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year as Purim, days turned from sorrow to joy, and the Jews bound it on their seed so that it would not fail (Esther 9:20-32). The teaching reminds that Purim is a memorial of the destruction of Israel’s enemies and of the Lord’s deliverance, not a day about presents (Rest of Esther 16:21-23). Mordecai was made next to the king, great among the Jews, seeking the wealth of his people and speaking peace to all his seed (Esther 10:3), and he confessed that God had done all these things (Rest of Esther 10:4-5). What was written before was written for our learning (Romans 15:4): days of sorrow now, and joy coming for those who stay in the commandments.
